source_read: PMC HTML, PMC5911369 (author manuscript of Drug Alcohol Depend 2017;180:241-259), read in full in my own browser tab: abstract, sections 1-7, Tables 1-5 with their notes, and the whole reference list (the part beyond 120,000 characters read with javascript on the same tab). The manuscript ends with the references: it carries no funding, conflict-of-interest or contributors statement.

claims.overstatement: None for the part attributed to this review: the claim labels it a narrative review, says 'without figures' and 'second-hand', and hedges the gene-environment point ('has been reported'). 'No longer detectable' renders the review's 'no longer a significant influence' fairly.
claims.note: Only the second-hand summary sentence and the last magnitude sentence cite this source, and both are supported. The review gives no twin heritability figure for any drug use disorder; the only twin variance figure it prints is for smoking abstinence (additive genetic influences 11%-74% of the variance, section 7), plus an unquantified 'highly heritable' nicotine-dependence phenotype (section 6), so the magnitude's wording ('for any drug use disorder') is exact. The review does not cite or discuss Kendler et al. (2012), the Swedish adoption study, anywhere in its text or reference list; its only 2012 Kendler citations are Dick & Kendler (2012a, 2012b), a review of gene-environment interaction in alcohol use disorders, cited without any heritability figure. So nothing in this source presents Kendler et al. (2012) as giving a heritability estimate.

anchors.locator: 3. Twin and Family Studies of Substance Use Disorder › 3.1 Genetic and Environmental Effects, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Narrative summary, no figures: twin studies report that initiation is influenced by genes and by shared and unique environment, consistently for tobacco, alcohol and cannabis; additive genetic influences are greater for progression (regular use, dependence); shared environment is no longer significant for regular use or dependence in adulthood but remains significant in adolescence; genetic influences on regular use and dependence remain after allowing for those specific to initiation; measures of progression and dependence vary between studies.

anchors.locator: 4. Genetic Association Studies › 4.1 Alcohol and Nicotine, 1st paragraph; 6. Limitations of SUD Genetic Epidemiology Studies, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Hundreds of markers reported for alcohol use disorder but hard to replicate consistently; SUD described as polygenic with many genes of small effect; replication inconsistent (few nicotine-dependence associations replicated), attributed to small effects, low power, differing phenotype measurement, genetic heterogeneity, ancestry differences between discovery and replication samples, and comorbidity.

anchors.locator: 4. Genetic Association Studies › 4.1 Alcohol and Nicotine, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Two studies (Kapoor et al., 2016; Salvatore et al., 2014) found significant associations of small effect between polygenic risk scores and alcohol dependence, the scores accounting for less than 1% of the total variance; a score association with age at onset of regular drinking also accounted for less than 1% (Vink et al., 2014); score associations were with dependence rather than initiation for alcohol and tobacco.

anchors.locator: 5. Non-Additive Genetic Mechanisms involved in SUD › 5.1 Gene-Environment Interplay, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Twin studies suggest genetic influences on alcohol-related behaviour vary with circumstances: higher genetic influence on late-adolescent alcohol use in urban settings, communities with more migration and more older adolescents and young adults; twin studies report greater genetic influence on adolescent smoking with low parental monitoring; a CHRNA5 variant's risk was lower with high parental monitoring; a smoking polygenic score's effect was larger with more lifetime trauma and smaller in neighbourhoods with high social cohesion.

anchors.locator: 5. Non-Additive Genetic Mechanisms involved in SUD, 1st paragraph; 5.1 Gene-Environment Interplay, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Additive genetic influences found so far have not accounted for a substantial share of the variance in SUD. Gene-environment correlation defined: parents and children share genes and the home, so parental genetic risk may also shape the child's environmental risk (the problem an adoption design addresses).

anchors.locator: 7. Conclusions and Future Directions, 3rd paragraph; 6. Limitations of SUD Genetic Epidemiology Studies, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: The only twin variance figure in the review: additive genetic influences account for 11%-74% of the variance of smoking abstinence (several twin studies). A 'highly heritable' nicotine-dependence factor phenotype is mentioned without a number. No heritability figure is given for any drug use disorder.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Methods; whole text and reference list
anchors.extracted: Narrative review: the literature 'was reviewed', with no search strategy, selection criteria or appraisal described. Kendler et al. (2012), the Swedish adoption study, is not cited in the text or the reference list; the 2012 Kendler citations are Dick & Kendler (2012a, 2012b), a gene-environment-interaction review cited in 5.1 (2nd and 3rd paragraphs) for kinds of environmental exposure and stress, with no heritability figure.

key_findings.note: Re-found blind: the only twin variance figure is 11%-74% for smoking abstinence (8 studies cited); the 'highly heritable' nicotine-dependence phenotype in section 6 has no number.
'Post-mortem' is the card's inference (human brain-tissue studies); the review does not use the word.

reporting_issues.note: Checked in Table 3: David S.P. (2012) 32,389 to 32,394; Tobacco and Genetics Consortium up to 74,035 to 74,037; Caporaso (2009) BBX row Male = 2060, TRPC5 row Male = 2062.
Checked: text N = 12,309; Table 5 lists KCNG2 and KCNC1 from Gelernter (2014), N = 5,390, African ancestry.
Checked: Table 4 Sherva (2016) cannabis dependence symptom count, n = 6,000, African ancestry, p = 4.32e-10, 1.33e-09, 2.13e-08, not replicated; not mentioned in the text.
Checked; Table 2 also has many '?' cells (effect allele, Zuo et al. rows), and 'ra62338789' is in Table 2.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high: no search, no appraisal, no figures, dopamine emphasis beyond the body's evidence.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract and Conclusions give dopamine genes a primacy that the reviewed genome-wide results do not show. The gap does not affect the claim, which uses only the twin summary, the replication point, the under-1% polygenic scores and the gene-environment examples.

missed: CORRECTION (known point settled), replication.timeline 2012 entry and replication.where_it_stands: they present Kendler et al. (2012) as 'a quantitative estimate with its population and era' and as an example of where heritability figures come from. Kendler et al. (2012) estimates no heritability (it gives rates and odds ratios of drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, risk-index odds ratios and a probability-scale interaction), and sc_kendler_2012 correctly records none. Prom-Wormley et al. (2017) does not cite Kendler et al. (2012) anywhere in its text or reference list (its 2012 Kendler citations are Dick & Kendler, 2012a/b), so the entry is an editors' cross-reference and should say so: 'National Swedish adoption study of registered drug abuse (Kendler et al., 2012): odds ratios in biological and adoptive relatives, no heritability estimate; not cited by this review'. where_it_stands should not name it as a source of heritability figures.

The section 3.1 twin summary that the claim uses (shared environment no longer significant for regular use or dependence in adulthood) cites Maes et al. (2017, Nicotine Tob Res 19:401-409), a twin-consortium paper co-authored by Prom-Wormley and Dick, whose reference entry lacks a title. The 'reliance on the authors' own studies' domain should name it alongside Prom-Wormley et al. (2015) and Dick & Kendler (2012).
